description: InfoSec World talks from InfoSec World 2024.

talks.title: CyberRisk TV LIVE from InfoSec World 2024 - Day 1 Intro
talks.teaser: A live expo-floor segment previews InfoSec World day one, the expo hall, and why open practitioner communities matter for security leaders.
talks.summary:
The segment opens from the InfoSec World 2024 expo floor in Lake Buena Vista, marking the event’s thirtieth year and setting expectations for day one. Guest Joshua Copeland describes his role leading managed security services—including SOC, MDR, and XDR—and his adjunct teaching in cybersecurity, AI, machine learning, ethics, and leadership. He compares the conference to larger shows like Black Hat or RSA, praising a smaller footprint with strong quality, roughly one hundred plus vendors, and an RSA-like energy without overwhelming scale.

The conversation turns to what he wants from the schedule: sessions about people and AI in managed security, because both remain persistent challenges. He frames his “unpopular opinions” lens as focusing on what goes wrong rather than hype about new startups and tooling, and stresses staying aware of the landscape even when not adopting everything immediately. Both participants emphasize in-person reconnection after the pandemic, bumping into peers across a contained venue, and a culture where practitioners share policies, research, and time on calls.

Copeland outlines a charity leadership book with about twenty contributors, with proceeds planned for the Cyber Human Initiative. He urges remote viewers to budget for next year’s October event, explore the vendor floor, and follow his LinkedIn presence. The host previews more CyberRisk TV interviews through the day and an afternoon wrap-up.

talks.title: Degrees Optional: Thriving in Cybersecurity Without Traditional Credentials - Suzanne ...
talks.teaser: Explains how people without an IT degree can break into cybersecurity through transferable skills and community connections.
talks.summary:
This short interview from InfoSec World 2024, recorded on the Expo floor in Florida, looks at how people without traditional credentials can move into cybersecurity. The guest, who runs a training center and began her career in web design before moving into teaching, presents a career change as something to plan carefully. She advises researching specific roles, starting where existing experience transfers, and recognizing that the broad cybersecurity professional role may not be a realistic first step.

The conversation then turns to skills-based hiring, which the guest says is replacing four-year degree requirements at many large US companies. She argues that durable skills such as communication, customer service and curiosity are often harder for employers to teach than technical ability. The host, who previously worked in senior security leadership, describes hiring people for basic skills rather than degrees and notes that most technologists learned by tinkering. For someone whose only experience is behind a retail or deli counter, the guest suggests reframing customer service work as relevant experience.

The main takeaway is the value of community. She recommends joining local meetups and professional chapters, and notes that most of her own roles came through people she already knew. The interview closes with reflections on the networking atmosphere at the conference and where viewers can find her career resources online.

talks.title: Vulnerability and Exposure Management - Brian Contos
talks.teaser: A Sevco executive explains how combining asset data and CVE feeds helps teams prioritize and verify vulnerability fixes.
talks.summary:
Brian Contos, chief strategy officer at Sevco Security, describes how the company started as an asset intelligence product and later added CVE data from several sources, so organizations get one prioritized view of their assets, vulnerabilities and exposures. He notes that many organizations now collect vulnerability information from at least six sources, such as endpoint detection tools and patch management platforms, not only traditional scanners. Scanners still matter for devices without agents or endpoint controls, such as printers, door locks and some critical infrastructure equipment.

He argues that a higher severity score does not always mean a higher priority. A score of five on a mission-critical system that lacks endpoint protection and has stale patching may deserve attention before a ten on a lab machine. Sevco's automated remediation validation pushes discovered issues into ticketing, SIEM or CMDB systems and tracks in real time whether they have been fixed, along with metrics on how long teams take. He describes a customer that used this during a recent endpoint outage to list affected mission-critical assets and watch the updates roll out.

He closes by saying this evidence helps security leaders brief executives and boards with less guesswork, and that dashboard screenshots work well for non-technical audiences. The practical takeaway is to measure remediation from discovery through verification, add business context to severity, and use shared data to reduce friction between security and IT teams.

talks.title: CyberRisk TV LIVE from InfoSec World 2024 - Day 1 Wrap-Up
talks.teaser: A live recap covers day-one keynotes, the new CISO track, and ways executive peer groups carry momentum beyond the expo floor.
talks.summary:
The segment closes the first day of a major information-security conference from an expo-floor broadcast studio. The conversation opens with reactions to morning keynotes, including an energizing opener and a dialogue about sitting in the chief information security officer role during a large corporate breach, with emphasis on team coordination, rest, and decisions leaders make to shield staff from prolonged crisis strain.

Much of the middle focuses on why in-person events matter for networking across a large vendor floor and for concentrated executive programming. The speakers describe the debut CISO-dedicated track, table-based discussions on cloud and shadow IT, and membership offerings that package policies, third-party risk guidance, and graphic incident-response playbooks built by practicing executives rather than generic advisory copy.

The close looks ahead to the second conference day and ongoing programs: organizational memberships, professional development credits, regional peer groups, and downloadable accelerators for teams retooling documentation. The practical takeaway is that conferences seed relationships and ideas, while structured collaboratives can turn shared lessons into reusable program artifacts through the rest of the year.

talks.title: CyberRisk TV LIVE from InfoSec World 2024 - Day 2 Intro
talks.teaser: Recaps InfoSec World 2024's first CISO track and day two, focusing on leadership and peer networking for security chiefs.
talks.summary:
This live Cyber Risk TV interview, filmed on the Expo floor at InfoSec World 2024, has host Dustin Sachs speaking with Chris ancharski, who leads national engagement and recruitment for Cyber Risk Collaborative. The pair open with a recap of day one, which featured the event's first CISO track. That track ran a full day of workshops and boardroom-style sessions built by and for the collaborative's members, covering regulation and compliance, cloud, critical infrastructure and CISO resilience.

The discussion then turns to day two, which opened with a keynote and a schedule of mainstage sessions. Ancharski says the conversations he hears from attendees centre on leadership, such as inspiring teams and explaining risk to boards in plain business language, with AI also prominent. He describes the collaborative's digital-first model, with year-round access for its more than 1,400 members, weekly regional and online gatherings, and task forces and working groups that will feed into next year's content.

The closing segment covers why the event suits budgeting for next year, mainly for its in-person networking and evening social contact that turn online connections into real relationships. The guest explains how to join the membership through the collaborative's website and names its engagement team as a contact point. The interview ends with an invitation for viewers to sign up for next year's event.

talks.title: Why Public & Private Sector Collaboration Matters - Parham Eftekhari
talks.teaser: Explains why private industry must help defend nationally critical systems and how a nonprofit bridge supports federal agencies.
talks.summary:
The conversation opens by framing cybersecurity work as part of national security, not only organizational risk. As societies depend on digitized services, most United States critical infrastructure sits in private hands, while nation-state adversaries target those systems. Government capacity alone cannot match that scale, so defender roles in industry carry national-level weight whether someone is new to the field or leads security for a large enterprise.

The middle section addresses mistrust between public and private actors and the need to separate political noise from career civil servants who stay in government service out of mission commitment. The Institute for Critical Infrastructure Technology describes its nonprofit role connecting technology partners, agencies, and policymakers in non-sales settings. A recent initiative focuses on Federal Civilian Executive Branch resilience across roughly 102 agencies that deliver everyday citizen services—from benefits and tax functions to parks and postal operations—where outages in water, banking, or healthcare matter immediately to ordinary Americans.

Practitioners should treat sector collaboration and trusted, nonpartisan education for decision-makers as complements to advocacy and lobbying. Balanced briefing helps legislators who cannot master every technical domain. The close points to open research, membership and event participation, and small individual contributions as practical ways to stay engaged rather than sidelined.

talks.title: What Makes a Strong Community - Parham Eftekhari
talks.teaser: Surveys what strong cybersecurity communities share and how year-round programs extend conference relationships into leadership growth.
talks.summary:
A floor interview at InfoSec World’s thirtieth anniversary frames community as a practical force for security leaders and practitioners, not an optional extra beside day jobs. The conversation contrasts conferences that stack technical sessions only with programs that deliberately mix education, relationship building, soft skills, leadership topics, and strategy—so attendees ranging from hands-on staff to aspiring and sitting CISOs can each find relevant value.

The guest argues that belonging to communities helps people validate decisions, refine strategies, decompress under pressure, and exchange puzzle pieces faster than any single organization can alone. He rejects the idea that practitioners want vendors locked out; members instead ask for qualified technology partners in formats where learning can map quickly to real challenges, while still segmenting conversations so roles interact appropriately.

The close maps how Cyber Risk Alliance stitches trade shows, digital media, research, and membership offerings into one ecosystem, including regional summits, collaborative working groups, expert channels, and large-scale in-person meetups beyond the annual show. Listeners hear what to pursue after the event ends, how feedback shapes programming, and which themes—consolidation risk, niche leader communities, and geopolitical threat briefings—are threading through the remainder of the conference.

talks.title: The Synergy of Leadership, Athlete Mindset, Cybersecurity, and Technology for Success ...
talks.teaser: Shows how Olympic athlete habits can guide goal-setting and career changes into cybersecurity.
talks.summary:
In this live interview from the Expo floor at InfoSec World 2024, Shannon, a three-time Olympian and managing partner at West Strategy Group, discusses the Medalist mindset. The idea applies tools that Olympic athletes use to business and personal goals. She co-created it with a fellow Olympian and presents five keys, starting with goals: defining your own version of the Olympics.

She describes a roughly fifteen-year pro career, three Games and a decade in the world top ten, and says consistency, meaning overcoming injuries and setbacks, is her proudest achievement. After leaving sport, she moved into consulting alongside a cybersecurity veteran, noting that cyber professionals share athletes' traits such as attention to detail, resilience and performance under pressure. She also cites creating a maternity policy for athletes, the first of its kind in her sport's national governing body.

For anyone unsure of their own goal, she suggests writing down what you would pursue with no expectations or commitments, then describing yourself in three words; her own were positive, persistent and trailblazer. Her broader point is that people switching into cybersecurity from other fields can translate past achievements into the value they bring to a new role.

talks.title: AI Revolution, Industry Secrets, & What’s Next for Cybersecurity -...
talks.teaser: Cyber Risk Alliance's events chief shares how InfoSec World is planned, what's next, and where AI fits.
talks.summary:
This Cyber Risk TV live interview, recorded on the Expo floor during InfoSec World 2024, marks the event's 30th anniversary. Host Dustin Sachs talks with John delmaro, executive vice president of events at Cyber Risk Alliance, about how the show has grown in attendance, exhibitors and technology providers since the pandemic and a hurricane disrupted earlier editions. Delmaro names an AI session featuring a go-to-market leader from OpenAI as the standout of the week.

The conversation then turns to how events are produced. Planning runs on a roughly twelve-month cycle that starts soon after each show closes, using attendee feedback to shape content and environments. Delmaro argues that a mid-sized scale lets attendees engage with practitioners more deeply than very large conferences allow. He outlines next year's move to late October, after Black Hat's August slot, and a possible family-friendly trip tied to a Disney setting. He also invites subject matter experts, case-study presenters and vendors to pitch ideas to his team.

Delmaro closes by pointing to other events his company runs: Identiverse, held each June in Las Vegas with more than 3,500 participants expected next year, and MSSP Alert Live in Austin in mid-October, now in its third year with over 500 attendees. His main advice to sponsors is to act as peers, attending sessions and networking in hallways rather than only staffing a booth.

talks.title: CyberRisk TV LIVE from InfoSec World 2024 - Day 2 Wrap-Up
talks.teaser: Day two highlights span hands-on workshops, executive tracks, networking culture, and ambitions for a more interactive 2025 event.
talks.summary:
The segment opens as a live-stream wrap from the expo floor on the second day of the conference, with the host noting that a half-day of sessions, an evening keynote, receptions, and Thursday workshops still lie ahead. The conversation turns to what stood out after two days on the floor: emphasis on people and hallway conversations, depth in executive-oriented programming, workshops with facilitators who walk attendees through practical steps, and keynote moments that attendees described as unusually strong.

The guest highlights hands-on workshops that leave people feeling ready for daily work, special tracks, and upcoming fireside programming tied to security for artificial intelligence. Both speakers discuss informal “hallway therapy,” peer commiseration, and a Women in Cyber breakfast that reportedly re-energized someone discouraged about the industry. They contrast the event with very large shows where expert voices are hard to find in the crowd, arguing that this venue still allows approachable contact with well-known practitioners despite substantial vendor and attendee scale.

Looking toward the next October edition and year-round engagement, they stress family-like peer connection, rising interactivity rather than passive attendance, regional communities, virtual events, and open channels for attendee ideas. The closing message is that programming, sponsors, and speakers co-build a long-running institution aimed at the discussions practitioners actually want to continue after they leave.
